In this lesson, you will learn about the operation of blocking oscillators.
INTRODUCTIONM
Blocking oscillators change DC into short, rectangular pulses that can be used as timing pulses to trigger other circuits.
Blocking oscillators do not produce sine waves like LC and RC oscillators.
Some radars use blocking oscillators as master clocks to control the many circuits needed to produce tracking pulses.
Let's begin the lesson on BLOCKING OSCILLATOR OPERATION...................

BLOCKING OSCILLATOR OPERATION
The blocking oscillator produces extremely narrow pulses and then stops for a relatively long period of time.
DEFINITION

INDUCTIVE KICKBACK - Inductive kickback is a spike of very high voltage, resulting from the almost instantaneous collapse of the magnetic field around an inductor when voltage is removed. A diode can absorb this energy and prevent damage to Q1.
The width of the output pulse also is dependent upon several factors. Vcc, R1, R2, R3, C2 and T1 all determine the frequency and the pulse width.
In this lesson, you will not be required to calculate the frequency of free-running blocking oscillators.
The purpose of triggered blocking oscillators is to improve the shape of input pulses. The input pulse can be any shape, provided it forward biases Q1.
There are two basic types of blocking oscillators:
Free-Running Blocking Oscillator Triggered Blocking Oscillator
Let's look at the operation of a free-running blocking oscillator first.
Free-Running Blocking Oscillator Triggered Blocking Oscillatorrr
When Vcc is applied, the NPN transistor starts to conduct.
Note: C1 is not used in free-running operation....
Collector current flows through the primary winding of T1, inducing voltage into the secondary (D1 is reverse biased).
The voltage on the secondary is limited by R3, and coupled through C2 to the base of Q1. This drives Q1 into saturation.
C2 charges quickly through the low emitter-to-base resistance of Q1 and assumes the charge shown.
When Q1 reaches saturation, collector current stops increasing. With no change in current, no voltage is coupled through T1.
C2 starts to discharge through R1 and R2. Notice C2's polarity.
C2 starts to discharge as positive charges flow from the battery through R1 and R2 to the capactior.

This causes the base of Q1 to become negative and drives Q1 into cutoff for a comparatively long period of time (D1 prevents inductive kickback) .

This time interval when C2 is discharging is called recovery time. The longer C2 takes to discharge, the longer the recovery time.
DEFINITION

INDUCTIVE KICKBACK - Inductive kickback is a spike of very high voltage, resulting from the almost instantaneous collapse of the magnetic field around an inductor when voltage is removed. A diode can absorb this energy and prevent damage to Q1.
When C2 is almost discharged, the reverse bias (negative) is removed from the base and Q1 starts to conduct again.
The process repeats and the result is sharp, narrow pulses that can be used to trigger other circuits.

The frequency of a blocking oscillator is called Pulse Repetition Frequency or (PRF) and depends on many factors.
Let's look now at the operation of a triggered blocking oscillator.
Triggered blocking oscillators cannot free-run. There is not any forward bias on the base of Q1.
Q1 cannot conduct until an input pulse of sufficient amplitude is coupled through C1 to supply the necessary forward bias.
As soon as current begins to flow through Q1, the magnetic field built up by the primary of T1 induces voltage into the secondary.
This secondary voltage charges C2 and quickly saturates Q1. This causes the voltage on the secondary (positive, regenerative feedback) to stop.
C2 discharges through R1, R3 and T1. This action reverse biases Q1 and collector current stops.
Q1 must receive another trigger pulse to begin conducting again. However, this pulse must not arrive before C2 is discharged or no output pulse occurs..
The blocking oscillator is often used to "clean up" signals when precise timing pulses are required.
Each input pulse produces one output pulse.
